summary:
Emberline: Harmonized Fire Calendar is a web app that turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire data for the California region into one consistent record of burning activity, from November 2000 to the latest month.
MODIS and VIIRS count fires differently, so their raw counts can't be joined. Emberline counts cell-days, meaning one 1 km cell with a detection on a day, once per sensor family. It maps VIIRS onto the MODIS scale per region using quantile mapping, which had a 22.2 holdout RMSE and 0.8 bias. MODIS counts are used before 2012 and calibrated VIIRS after. The sensor of origin no longer matters.
Users draw or enter an area and a date range. They get a month-by-year calendar, anomalies against the historical median, a watch badge, a season tracker, key figures, and CSV and chart downloads.
This gives emergency responders, scientists and land managers a way to see which periods and years burned most, and how now compares with history. The app states its limits openly, including that the latest month is provisional.
details:
What it does and how it works

Emberline turns NASA FIRMS active-fire detections for the California region into one monthly record from November 2000 to the latest month. The data come from two sensor families that can't be compared directly, MODIS and VIIRS.

  • Counting unit: a cell-day is one 1 km cell with at least one kept detection on a day, counted once per sensor family. This removes the pixel-size and extra-satellite effects.
    • a month-by-year calendar in counts, anomaly and month-to-month difference views
    • key figures
    • a watch badge
    • a season tracker
    • a recent-activity view
    • a comparison of two areas or two periods
    • downloads of CSV files and chart images
  • Statistics: baselines and anomalies are computed at query time from zero-filled series.

Benefits and intended impact

Responders, scientists, land managers and firefighters can see which periods and years burned most, and how now compares with history, without sensor artifacts in the series. The aim is a trustworthy shared picture of burning activity as MODIS nears the end of its life.

Tools used

  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, DuckDB, pandas, pyarrow, numpy, scipy, shapely.
  • Front end: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL with Terra Draw, Apache ECharts, Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui, TanStack Query, zod.
  • Tests: pytest and Hypothesis, Vitest and fast-check, with axe accessibility checks.
  • Delivery: one Docker image. The data files are not in git and come from a Hugging Face dataset repo.
  • AI tool: Kiro built the code from a spec. The data pipeline was built outside Kiro.
  • Hardware: development was on a Mac. Hosting is DEFAULT (confirm): Render.

What is creative

  • Cell-days as a common unit, instead of scaling raw counts.
  • Per-region quantile mapping instead of one global factor.
  • Calendar views: a calendar that shows anomalies against each month's own history.
  • Comparison and sharing: area and period comparison on one shared colour scale, and share links that keep the area and dates in the web address.
  • Property-based tests that check the statistics.

Factors considered

  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes, keyboard use, and screen-reader text.
  • Honest limits: the latest month is shown as provisional. Small areas are noisy after 2012. The data come from filtered, un-harmonized detections. No claim is made about a state-boundary mask.
  • Time convention: a fixed UTC-8 stated everywhere.
  • Not shown: uncertainty intervals, because the calibration error file wasn't delivered.
  • Data separation: tests use synthetic data, never the real data.
